A couple of interesting posts in @C_Barraud's packed Thursday Brief indicate that while China’s stock rescue package got a shrug, as I posted on Tuesday, the US midterm results got a rally.

After Beijing rolled out its 2024-style support tools on Monday, the CSI 300 slipped 0.2% Tuesday and the tech-heavy Star 50 fell 3.8%. Then Democrats swept both chambers of Congress, and the CSI 300 jumped 2.3% Wednesday, its best day since July. It added 0.3% Thursday to 4,113, up 2.6% in two sessions.

Hong Kong followed with a bigger move Thursday:
▪️ The Hang Seng rose 3.7%, its best day since February 2025 (+4.0% on February 21, 2025, during the DeepSeek rally). It’s now up about 8% from its October 22 low.
▪️ The Hang Seng Tech rose 5.6%, the most since February 2025, per Bloomberg.
▪️ Alibaba and Tencent each rose more than 7%, and Meituan added 6.8%.

Investors are reading the result as a risk to the US AI hardware trade and rotating into value. China’s internet platforms are about as cheap as large-cap tech gets: Bloomberg notes the Hang Seng Tech traded at 13 times forward earnings last month, the lowest since 2024. Bloomberg Intelligence’s Marvin Chen sees three rotations at once. Money is moving out of Korea and Taiwan into China, into value after China was “stuck at trough valuations” while the rest of the world rallied, and away from “tech hardware and pure AI plays.”

The same rotation shows up in the US. Bespoke says 91.5% of consumer discretionary stocks are above their 50-day averages, the highest in at least a year, compared with 35.5% of tech stocks.

Positioning added fuel. Short selling was 32% of Hong Kong’s turnover on Tuesday, the highest in more than three years, according to Bloomberg. Lotus Asset Management’s Hao Hong calls the move “one of the biggest short squeezes in recent years.” The cost of hedging the Hang Seng Tech fell to its lowest since July, and options volume on the Tracker Fund hit a one-year high as bullish bets dominated.

To be fair to Beijing, Bloomberg also reported stepped-up national-team buying and buybacks Wednesday, so the policy floor is perhaps part of this. 

A caveat: Big up days aren’t reliable bottoms. Since 2000, the Hang Seng has had 53 separate days of 3.5% or more. While a month later it was higher 62% of the time (median +3.0%), three months later it was a coin flip: higher 53% of the time, with a median gain of 1.5%.

So after doing my thing with Jack Farley and stewing a bit here's some thoughts about dc's 

Let's presume that the narrative is correct and a marked slowdown in data center build has occured.  One could say it had occured anyway and without the political catalyst we had reached peak growth but let's stick with the idea that the result of the election is stalled data center build out.  

Literally all suppliers of goods and services for BUILDING new are fucked. No way around that outcome.

Let's strawman three formations of data center companies

1. Fully built already AND not planning and never priced to plan to build more (not sure if any exist). They have compute which may become scarce and prices bid up
2. Pure new build company with projects in the hopper but none built so far.  Not sure if any exist but they are fucked. Their stocks are 100% on the come.  They may have debt or committments which depend on revenues from compute that won't get built.
3. Combination of both. With obviously the mix mattering a lot. Some benefit of compute scarcity offset by future build revenue dropping and/or delayed. 

So let's deal with existing compute.  Clearly it will be scarce and prices could be bid up. IFF The buyer of compute can pay for it and or pass it on to the end buyer.    The buyer of compute is largely the frontier models as the marginal pricer.  I see that buyer burning compute to train their models with no revenue and some revenue from model sales to end users but probably very very little pricing power particularly given the slower model improvement in a scarce and expensive compute environment.  
That dynamic will increase cash burn and financing needs of frontiers. 

I can't see how the compute scarcity is net good for overall cohort profits with picks and shovels directly impacted negatively. With existing compute having some upside.  With future compute companies viability threatened. With frontiers in trouble unless they can raise prices and sell expensive tokens and slow model development 

At the same time a stall will reduce issuance volume for compute build which has been huge.

Equity risk premiums could contract while earnings expectations has to go down a lot for the whole cohort except for those narrow companies with built capacity and no other negatives.

Of course the frontier models pricing power may be poor due to Chinese models as well.

$COHR earnings transcript TLDR:

Q: On $LITE + $MRVL merger.

A. Customers will prefer an independent optical supplier without competitive conflicts (opportunity for other merchant laser suppliers)

Q: Loop Capital asked about 2028 laser industry oversupply.

A: No oversupply risk by 2028. Coherent’s entire current internal InP production is consumed by its own products while its expanding capacity.

Q: On Chinese laser competition for CPO UHP lasers

A: “We really only have one competitor” (hinting at $LITE). 

Q: On financing concerns for capacity expansion during this market scare

A: Customer LTAs have prepayments, which are used for product capacity orders

2027 completely sold out, LTAs extend to 2030, customers placing orders into 2028.

Q: On laser technology for CPO scale up from Bernstein, whether it’s VCSELs or CW lasers.

A: CW for CPO scale out and scale up for 2026-2027.

2029-2030 sees scale in and chip to chip using micro-VCSELs, and 2028 opportunities for NPO scale up.

So technology of choice is CW for CPO.

- Coherent is seeing pricing power and raising margin targets, supporting view optical players get additional leverage for margin expansion

- Massive new $20B 5Y LTA, anchored by UHP CW lasers, with other optical products mixed in

- demand comes from growth in DC and conversion of copper interconnects to optics. The latter is bandwidth requirements, independent of DC growth.

slower compute growth can coexist with sharply rising optical content per system

TLDR:

- nothing quite showing optical demand like $20B in LTAs anchored by high power lasers from 1 customer alone (not your frontier labs type commitments)

- no industry wide laser oversupply risk by 2028 for InP lasers/EML 

- financing funded by revenue from LTAs and purchase orders.

- doesn’t see Chinese competition for high end lasers, commentary casts doubts over China capability + capacity expansion claims

- CW lasers weapon of choice for CPO, blended margins going up for optical players

- optics more isolated in the event of a DC slowdown 

Quite wild to see fundamentals of optical players improve so much, while overall valuations crash.

Venice burned about $1.06M of $VVV in October, its biggest regular month so far. 

The bad news is that total supply is still going up, because more new VVV came out in October than got burned.

However...

That math changes soon in January 2027. 

Right now about 19K new VVV hits the market every day from staking rewards and unlocks. 

Most of the scheduled unlocks end on January 1, so that drops to around 6K a day. If burns stay the same, they cover about a quarter of new supply instead of 7.5%, roughly 3x the impact.

Usage is growing fast too. Venice says @AskVenice went from about 250B to over 1T AI tokens (the small chunks of text AI reads and writes) a day in October.

There are two catches though, and both are bad for holders.

1, Usage isn't the same as paid revenue. Even after January, burns need to grow about 4x before supply really shrinks.

2. VVV holders don't own any of Venice's revenue. The company decides how much to burn, and it can change that.

So I'm cautiously bullish, but only for a window. 

Investor tokens start unlocking in July 2027 and could add up to ~6K VVV a day, which is about as much as all the new supply after January. 

So January to July is the six months where burns face the least new supply they'll see for years, and if they can't catch up to it then, I don't think they ever will.

Huge relief for $MARA.

FERC approved $MARA’s Long Ridge acquisition today (EC26-92). Good to see the IMM’s spurious BlackRock/Vanguard challenge get the Heisman. FERC also turned down the request to condition approval on keeping the plant’s output in PJM. Solid.

The deal: $1.512B enterprise value for ~0.5 GW of gas generation (485 MW authorized, 505 MW nameplate) and ~$144M of annualized adj. EBITDA, about 10.5x. Recent PJM gas plant deals went at about 7x (Talen 6.7x, Vistra 7x, NRG 7.5x), which would put the plant alone at ~$1.0B. MARA is paying ~$0.5B more for the land, gas wells, rail and expansion option. MARA keeps ~$900M of Long Ridge debt in place and needs ~$610M of cash, which the $600M of BTC-backed loans it drew in August are meant to cover. I’d expect it to close by the Nov 30 outside date.

Debt math: ~$1.9B of MARA’s $2.3B convert stack is zero coupon, so total post-close cash interest is roughly $140M: ~$58M on the Coinbase and Two Prime loans, ~$76M on Long Ridge’s own debt (the 8.75% notes alone are $52.5M) and ~$7M on the converts. Judging the deal on its own: the debt that finances it (Long Ridge’s ~$76M plus ~$46M on the new BTC loans) costs ~$123M a year against $144M of EBITDA, about 1.2x. The upside is expansion.

MARA talks about 600 gross MW of AI load at the site. That appears to include the existing 200 MW of grid load (on top of the 505 MW plant that sells into PJM). AEP’s 2025 filing proposed reconductoring the feeder serving a customer at the Hannibal station to go from 100 to 200 MW, for about $0.5M, targeting about nine months from PJM first seeing the need to in-service. The station ties into four 138 kV lines and once fed a 540 MW smelter, which is encouraging, but nothing is signed. To get from 200 to 600 MW, AEP would likely need to add a second feed or upgrade lines, or MARA would build on-site generation, which raises turbine availability questions. I can’t find a public study of how much more the grid connection can carry. AEP Ohio’s data center tariff also requires large customers to pay for at least 85% of contracted capacity for up to 12 years, if it applies here. Still, an energized site with fuel, land and a 138 kV hub may beat waiting in ERCOT’s queue.

It’s unclear whether the Hannibal buildout goes through the Starwood JV, where MARA would keep up to 50%. That will decide how much of the 600 MW upside MARA owns. Each 100MW developed at a 7% cap rate and $2M/MW rent could be $1.5B+ of value creation, so it's a big variable and explains why they paid ~$500M above the 7x multiple for the extra capacity.

Next catalyst, possibly at closing or just after: a signed lease.

For those unfamiliar with $STAA, STAAR Surgical is the global leader in implantable lenses for vision correction, an alternative to LASIK that doesn’t require removing corneal tissue. When it comes to your eyes, you’re not going to put something inside them that hasn’t been tested in other people’s eyes for at least 5 to 10 years. Competitors have faced safety problems with implantable lenses in the past that where considered “the next big thing”, making STAAR’s long clinical track record a substantial competitive advantage.

I initially recommended $STAA at $17.50, following the proposed $30.75 acquisition by Alcon, which was opposed by Broadwood Partners, a hedge fund owning approximately 30% of the company, on the grounds that the offer was too opportunistic.

Yesterday’s earnings further reinforced my investment thesis. Revenue reached $83.4M, representing 21% underlying growth, with China up 31% and Europe up 31%. Adjusted EBITDA improved to $14.4M, net income reached $5.6M, and cash increased to $206M with zero debt. For the first nine months of 2026, revenue reached $270.5M and adjusted EBITDA $58.8M. Management also authorized a $50M share buyback.

Gross margins remain under pressure at 70.9%, but management expects improvement beginning in Q4 and continuing into 2027.

The important story is how much the business has changed since the acquisition offer. If you’ve followed my tweets, you know that the underlying business has improved substantially. I would argue that the company’s situation today is many times better than when the $30.75 offer was made and subsequently rejected.

Just before the latest earnings, Steve Cohen’s Point72 acquired approximately 5% of the company at around $29 per share. Despite the stock’s recent 45% rally, we’re only now back to roughly the price at which Point72 established its position.

With a strong balance sheet, recovering profitability and growing demand for its products, I believe there’s considerably more upside. It’s not hard for me to see $STAA reaching $50 per share with patience.

Following its 45% rise, $STAA is now my second-largest position.

hard to articulate what i'm thinking here after Tuesday, but i'll give it a shot because i think it's important to understand the seismic shift occurring within both political parties in the US:

Democrats fucked themselves up in the lead up to 2024 because they over-rotated on stupid social issues as a way to stand against Trump. they thought this was legitimately their best strategy and it became their entire brand to a lot of people

ofc, it was a disaster. most people don't mind what others do in their own homes, but they don't want things forced down their throats

but what's interesting about the big wins on Tuesday is the Democrats didn't win (or even run) on these issues. though their opponents on the right tried to saddle them with that baggage, it simply didn't work

the messages which broke through were around 1) affordability, 2) ending the Iran war (which has also harmed affordability), 3) addressing somewhat vague concerns around AI-related job loss (most tangibly observed in unmitigated data center build out), and 4) stemming the substantial observable corruption within the Trump administration

social issues were almost completely absent from the Democratic platform. further, the winning platform also didn't really originate meaningfully from the traditional DNC elites. it bubbled up through a lot of younger upstart candidates, many of whom could seriously be credible as candidates for POTUS in 2028

so it's likely the Democratic talent vacuum has ended, and the Republican talent vacuum is now beginning

as a result, it's quite possible that Democrats WON'T have to go further left on social issues to recruit the votes needed to win POTUS in 2028. IF they can hold on this, then it also simultaneously makes their platform more attractive to relatively centrist Republicans who are also fed up with all of the aforementioned issues

so if Dems don't fuck up on social issues and on immigration (i.e., they need to have a credibly strong immigration policy), then they don't need the extreme left to win anymore

in isolation, this seems like it would break the two party system, but the response will be that the Republican Party moves further to the left on some issues. nativist and race-driven platforms won't work because they are inherently exclusionary. most normal people not on this site in 2026 are also not driven by racial factors in their voting decisions

so, tl;dr- big shifts are coming to both parties. Democrats will actually move more centrist on social issues while becoming more meaningfully progressive on economic issues. Republicans tbd, but they also probably move more towards the center back to economic issues the working class cares about (not just social issues)

like it or not, the race for 2028 starts now 🇺🇸

Management also highlighted accelerating progress in autonomous transportation, expecting approximately 700 fully driverless vehicles operating on Uber's platform by year-end and more than 2,000 in 2027, as the company increasingly focuses on commercializing robotaxi services at scale.

4. AMD $AMD has dramatically increased its unconditional purchase commitments to $48.8B, up 4x from $12.2B at the end of 2025 and $30.3B in June, according to its latest 10-Q filing, highlighting the enormous supply chain investments required to support its accelerating AI infrastructure business. Approximately $33.4B of these commitments are due by the end of 2027, primarily covering semiconductor wafers, advanced memory, substrates, and packaging capacity. AMD also disclosed $6.2B in cloud computing commitments, $13.3B in data center leases it expects to assign or sublease to partners, and up to $8.5B in guarantees covering partners' lease and debt obligations. The deal would have allowed Tencent to access advanced semiconductor technology that remains restricted within China, prompting U.S. officials to raise national security concerns with Oracle. Meanwhile, senior Chinese officials reportedly urged Tencent to prioritize domestic semiconductor suppliers, adding pressure from Beijing. Although overseas AI chip leasing remains permitted under existing regulations, the agreement was reportedly abandoned amid mounting geopolitical pressure from both governments.

Non-GAAP operating income reached $550M, ahead of the $527M estimate, while gross margins expanded 184 basis points to 40.6%, reflecting improving profitability. The sizable insider purchase represents a notable vote of confidence from Intel's chief executive as the company continues executing its turnaround strategy, expanding its AI and data center business, and investing in its next-generation foundry manufacturing capabilities. The transaction highlights Tan's willingness to increase his personal exposure to Intel's long-term performance as investors assess the sustainability of its recovery.
